question: A previously healthy 6-month-old girl is brought to the physician by her mother for occasional “eye crossing.” Her mother says that the symptoms have become worse, especially before bedtime. The patient was born via cesarean delivery at 37-weeks' gestation and has met all developmental milestones. The patient's immunizations are up-to-date. She is at the 50th percentile for both length and weight. Her temperature is 36.7°C (98°F), pulse is 130/min, respirations are 40/min, and blood pressure is 90/60 mm Hg. Visual acuity is 20/20 in both eyes. There is an asymmetric corneal light reflection. When the left eye is covered, the right eye moves laterally. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient?

options.opd: Cyclopentolate eye drops on the left

enhanced_information: The most appropriate next step in the management of this patient is to measure intraocular pressure to rule out glaucoma, given the presence of possible sixth cranial nerve palsy. Cyclopentolate eye drops on the left can help assess for accommodative esotropia, leading to reassurance and follow-up if needed.
analysis: The core medical principle in this case is to evaluate the possible causes of the eye crossing, which could be related to sixth cranial nerve palsy or accommodative esotropia. Given the asymmetric corneal light reflection and lateral movement of the right eye when the left eye is covered, there is a concern for sixth cranial nerve palsy. The most appropriate next step is to measure intraocular pressure to rule out glaucoma, which can present similarly to sixth cranial nerve palsy. Cyclopentolate eye drops on the left can help assess for accommodative esotropia, but given the asymmetric findings, ruling out glaucoma takes precedence. Reassurance and follow-up can be provided based on the results of the intraocular pressure measurement.
